text:
[SASRec](https://arxiv.org/abs/1808.09781) already adaptively combines historical interactions; its paper reports greater focus on recent actions in sparse datasets and longer dependencies in dense datasets. Adding pooled history therefore does not by itself establish sustained-interest modeling. Established precedents include [FPMC](https://archives.iw3c2.org/www2010/pub/pdfs/RendleFreudenthaler2010-FPMC.pdf), combining user preferences with first-order transitions, and [Fossil](https://cseweb.ucsd.edu/~jmcauley/pdfs/icdm16a.pdf), combining normalized historical item embeddings with personalized higher-order Markov components. A last-item residual is a useful short-term control, though it is not equivalent to full FPMC.

Recommended ablation: unchanged SASRec versus SASRec plus a padding-masked uniform history mean, normalized exponential mean with weights exp(-λ·lag), or last-item embedding. Use identical history windows, embedding tables, residual scaling, training settings and tuning budgets; compute every training-position pool causally. Exponential pooling approaches uniform pooling at λ=0 and last-item pooling as λ grows, making these informative endpoints. Include pooling-only and older-history-only controls: gains matching the last-item residual suggest recency; gains surviving removal of recent items better support historical information. These are proposed experiments, not published findings for this benchmark.

Keep the pinned four-category macro validation HR@10 and candidate sets unchanged. Diagnose popularity using training-frequency baselines, target-frequency strata and recommendation concentration. [Sampled-metric research](https://research.google/pubs/on-sampled-metrics-for-item-recommendation/) shows sampled rankings need not preserve full-catalog model ordering. [RepeatNet](https://arxiv.org/abs/1812.02646) explicitly models recommending previously consumed items; that mechanism cannot directly explain unseen-item recommendation gains. Repeated interests across different items remain plausible, but require evidence beyond aggregate HR@10.
